Who is responsible for
looking after the ventilation and heating of
<2918
Supply-Public Works

this chamber? After a time it is usually so hot and stuffy that it is not fit for people to live in.
Employees of the Department of Public Works operate the equipment under the direction of the officials of the house.

That does not give us
very much information. Is anybody responsible in general for looking after this chamber and the other rooms in order that they may be properly ventilated, not overheated, and that the air, at least in this chamber, may be fit to breathe? Surely there is somebody whose duty it is to superintend this work. The matter has been referred to a number of times in the house but we do not seem to get anywhere. Is there someone on whom the minister could place the responsibility?

I do not see the Sergeant-at-Arms in his seat. There is a thermometer on his desk. He is supposed to keep an eye on the temperature indicated by that thermometer and if it gets too high, to have some fresh air let in or, if it gets too low, to see that the temperature is increased.

The real difficulty is the
condition of the atmosphere. Some times it is not only the heat but the bad air which i? oppressive. The place is not properly ventilated. We have an expensive set of machinery for ventilating the building. I do not know what type it is but either the machinery is faulty or those who are operating it do not know their business. That is the long and the short of the matter. The situation is serious because while we sit here during the session, we almost invariably get a headache or feel some other depression. With this expensive machinery we ought to have satisfactory ventilation and we are not getting it.

This is something to
which I have been devoting some thought and time in connection with some of my other duties. The system is called the combination plenum and exhaust system. There are fans that are supposed to suck in the pure air and other fans which are supposed to draw out the impure air.

The impure air fan doe3
not work.

This building is a good
deal like other buildings which have been erected under the supervision of the best architects procurable; it is well constructed After a number of people have been in all the galleries and in the house from three o'clock in the afternoon until perhaps ten o'clock in the evening and a number of members on all sides of the house have been talking a good deal, the air is not as good at ten o'clock in the evening as it was when the house opened at three o'clock in the afternoon. My hon. friend will notice that now there is nothing to complain about. I see we are all agreed on that.
What would happen if we called the divorce bills?

Of course, you cannot expect it to remain like this all the time. To be serious, I am told that in practically every building after it has been occupied five or six or seven hours, even under the best regulated system off ventilation known to architectural science, the air becomes not as fresh as it was at the beginning. It is the same with any theatre. I understand that the system here is one to which great consideration was given at the time of the construction of this building, and it is said to be in repair at the present time. Only recently we have adopted the system of gauging the temperature by a thermometer, which is under the supervision of a very careful official of the house, who makes it one of his duties to regulate the temperature.

No plenum system will work if an outside door is open, because that lets the draught in and puts the whole arrangement out of order. The plenum system in a building of this kind will not work, and you might as well make up your mind to that, but we might get some relief from letting in the fresh air.

I suppose that, like all
questions of a more or less scientific nature, there are differences of opinion about that.

Not much difference of
opinion about that.
I think so, if I may say so. According to my information, our system is one of the best available, but, of course, if a door is open in very cold weather you will get a draught through any building.
That is not the point.

It is the point, if I may say so, in connection with this building. Those sitting particularly in the vicinity

Supply-Public Works
where I now stand can feel a draught on the back of their neck practically every time the outside door and the door over here are open at the same time.

The point is that opening
that door disturbs the draught of air that is supposed to ventilate the chamber. If you have a room that is hermetically sealed, you can ventilate it very well by the plenum system, but opening an outside door and letting in a draught disturbs the whole arrangement. I suggest that the minister consider that question with a view to installing a. better system. We shall get no relief otherwise.

It is a matter in which I am very much interested because I have myself experienced the discomforts which hon. gentlemen complain of, and if I can find any way of improving the system I shall be very glad to do it. Proper ventilation is most essential to the health and comfort of everybody who has to spend any time in this house.
Close up the session in two weeks and hon. members will be able to get all the ventilation they want free.

Those who sat in the old chamber will remember that the ventilation was not very good, and that it was very often discussed. But so far as the acoustics were concerned, the old chamber was far superior to this. For instance, I have had to content myself with hearing only half the explanation just given by the minister on this question of ventilation; I could not make out half of what he said, and half of what is said from the far corner of the house is not audible at this end, so I hope the minister has not given up entirely the task of improving the acoustics of this chamber. This is a magnificent chamber and a credit to the architect, but I am Sony to say that so far as the acoustics are concerned it is not a success, and we at this end are able to hear only very imperfectly what is said from the other end, and vice versa. That was admitted, and the members of the cabinet had to move more towards the centre of the chamber so that they could be better heard at that far end, but their moving down has been our loss, because we are not able to hear the explanations given by the ministers. So if anything can be done to improve the acoustics of this chamber, I hope it will be done because it is very much needed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I might be permitted
to say a word here. While the acoustic properties of the chamber are not all that may be desired, if hon. gentlemen would keep
better order and less conversation were carried on in the chamber, hon. members would b*. able to hear the ministers and to hear each other when speaking in committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There is no difficulty
in hearing the minister now that we have order in the chamber.

There is something in
what the chairman says. The acoustic properties are greatly improved when the members of the house are making a reasonable effort to hear what is being said, and when not too many of them are talking at the one time.

In the old chamber, at confederation, the Speaker's chair was at the end of the chamber, but with the increased membership it was found necessary to transfer it to the centre of the chamber, and that improved the acoustics very considerably. Have the experts considered the question of moving the Speaker's chair to the centre of the room and arranging the seats in a sort of semi-circle around it, so that everyone would be facing the Speaker and the Speaker would be facing the members?

That has been considered. Models have been made and a plan was endeavoured to be worked out along that line, but the objection to that is that if the Speaker's chair were opposite to where I am now standing, the voice probably would not carry to that corner. I am told that that plan is not feasible, and the experts consider that the present system is the best they know of at the present time.

The system I suggest has been tried at Washington and at the Palais Bourbon in Paris, and in many other capitals in Europe.
Supply-Public Works

M<r. ELLIOTT: My hon. friend is familiar with what happens in Paris. The speakers go to a certain point in the chamber when they are going to address the house, and they all speak from the same point. It is quite feasible then. The acoustic properties can be improved when the speaking all takes place from the same point and the voice carries reasonably in the same direction, but that plan is quite unworkable when speakers are speaking from all over the chamber.

This is an important
matter, Mr. Chairman, I do not think the ventilation can be improved by simply opening the doors. I have a great deal of sympathy for the officers of the house and others whose duties oblige them to remain in the chamber throughout the sitting. I am sure the attendance of hon. members in the house would be much better if the ventilation were improved. In my judgment large air tubes should be installed from the ceiling to the outside through which the vitiated air would be withdrawn by electric fans. As to the acoustics of the chamber, I think two years ago a vote was placed in the estimate to effect an improvement in this respect. I understand that an expert reported that the acoustic properties were all right. I should like that expert to sit here day after day as we do in an effort to hear what is being said. Those whose hearing is normal find it very difficult and at times impossible to distinguish a speaker addressing the chair from either end of the chamber. Undoubtedly something is radically wrong with the acoustics, and it seems to me that the only remedy would be to install radio distributors. Then we should be able to hear any hon. member without effort.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to
endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. MacNutt). It is most important that we should hear what is going on. That is what we are here for.
Louder.

In the house of Lords there
is a telephone on each member's desk. Whether that is for the purpose of making audible to each member the debates in the chamber I do not know; but I do not recall seeing a similar system in the House of Commons.

The minister has justified

speechtext:
The next two items
for Rideau Hall were adopted at a previous sitting of the committee.
Telephone service-$100,000.

What is
included in this large expenditure?

This covers the rental
for the fiscal year of the telephone connections throughout the several departments in the city of Ottawa.

Are the
telephone costs of Rideau Hall and the governor general's office included in this item?

That is correct.
Mr. GARLAND (Bow River)- I find in part V-32 of the Auditor General's report for 1927 an item of $378.05 for the governor general's office and Rideau Hall for telephones. I turn to part V

31 of the same report and I find an expenditure of $355.20 for the governor general's office and Rideau Hall for telephones, direct lines, and so on. Then at part G-3 another item, telegrams and telephones amounting to $4,020.32, again for Rideau Hall. The total is $4,753.57, most of which would appear to be for telephone

Supply-Public Works
messages. What is the reason for this extraordinary telephone bill for Rideau Hall? There may be some good reason for it. How much is the estimate for this year?

That is part of the
expenses of the building from and to which telephone messages are sent. It is not in connection with this building. What my hon. friend refers to I take it, although I have not looked over the details specially, would cover the various telephone calls and telerams from the governor general's office.

That
explanation is hardly good enough I find for example in the same item of the Auditor General's report at part V-31 that the total cost of telephones for the Prime Minister in respect of the House of Commons is only $57.96, and he has another small bill in connection with the External Affairs department. Even the Prime Minister's telephone calls do not nearly approximate those of Rideau Hall. I cannot understand why there is such a heavy expenditure. The minister has not yet told the committee how much of this $100,000 will be devoted this year to the Rideau Hall telephones.
Will the minister explain how it is that there are three or four different accounts for telephones? Why should there be so many.

These subdivisions are
made by the Auditor General. He subdivides them under the different headings and is, I understand, responsible for the classifications that appear here. Of course, they all have to be passed on by him.

I want to say a
few words in regard to this item. We all appreciate the minister's seriousness in dealing with these items; he is more serious than any other minister, and he realizes the importance of the matters involved. But he must realize at the same time that there is a rumour abroad that there is great waste in connection with the administration here. In my opinion, if there were put under one item all the automobiles in use by every person connected with the administration, and the same in the matter of telephones, the government could satisfy the demands of nearly all those who are asking for public buildings. Here we have an item of $100,000, and I am sure that if the minister went through it carefully with a view to eliminating unnecessary expenditures he could provide a post office for my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), in Sydenham, and one for
Camrose as well. I would ask the minister to turn to two pages which have been referred to in the Auditor General's report for 1927. There he will find a long list of office telephones. I have no doubt that if he went through that list he would discover a great many telephones which are absolutely unnecessary; they could be done without, especially when people are unable to obtain proper postal service throughout the country. He will also find, if he consults this book, a list of private telephones in private residences throughout Ottawa. Many of these telephones can be justified, but I will guarantee that a great many of them cannot. There are seventeen ministers who have telephones in their private residences and apartments; there are also twenty-seven deputies and sixty-three sub-deputies who have private telephones in their private residences, paid for by the government of Canada. Take the various departments: Agriculture with nine sub-deputies; Justice with five; the Post Office with seven; the Public Works with six and the Railways with six. If the minister or his deputy would take these two pages and go over them carefully he could eliminate enough of absolutely unnecessary expenditure to provide a post office in Camrose, one in Sydenham and one or two others, about the necessity for which we have heard.
And Pictou.

Pictou, if you like. If the minister will take the automobiles used by the officials and deputy officials and those connected with the administration and put them all under one head, I guarantee he will be able to supply a post office in every place where a demand is made for one. With this $100,000 we have here I am sure he could provide three or four post offices. I cannot understand why so many persons need private telephones to be paid for by the government. I grant you that eveiy department should have a certain number; for example, work must be done on Saturdays and on Sundays and at night. But why should we pay for private telephones for six and seven subdeputies and sometimes the secretaries of ministers? I cannot understand it. I repeat, I would refer the minister to these two pages of the Auditor General's report, and I would ask him to go over them carefully with a view to cutting out unnecessary expenditure. If he did so now, and again next year, he would be able to provide a post office for every member who asked for one.

I know my hon. friend
is serious in making these suggestions and
Supply-Public Works

perhaps I should devote a minute or two to him; because the matter is important if what he says is correct. In the first place, it is not correct that there is great waste, nor do I think it is correct that there is a general impression throughout the country to that effect. What is the test? Look at the amount of money paid out in the last fiscal year in this department and compare it with what was paid out in other years and you will see whether there is great waste or not. I would call my hon. friend's attention to a statement I made the other day in answer to a somewhat similar criticism: that in this country in 1913, which was a quite normal year, this department, with Canada doing a trade of $1,048,000,000, paid out in cash in this particular department $18,884,000. Last year on the other hand, with wages greatly increased, with cost of materials increased by at least 50 per cent, and with the cost of practically every service also increased, the total expenditure in this department, to provide for a trade of $2,357,000,000, was $17,408,000. Let my hon. friend get this into his head, because I know he believes what he has been saying with reference to these rumors, which perhaps he has been encouraging. He believes that we are spending in this department more money than was spent years ago by his friends whom he has lauded to the skies. But he is wrong. He also believes that the business of the country is not as good to-day as it was years ago. In that particular also he is wrong. Just let me put the matter in figures which my hon. friend and everyone else in this house who is similarly minded can understand. With a business in Canada a little over a third of what it is to-day the government of this country in 1913 spent 50 per cent more in this department than we spent last year-and last year was the highest year but one since this government came into power. Let me give the figures so that we shall have the matter threshed out. In 1912-13-
We must be getting along too quickly.
You cannot get along too quickly if there are misunderstandings.
Go on.

We shall get along more
quickly when we appreciate the facts. For the year 1912-13 the total amount paid out in this department was $18,884,000; for the last fiscal year before the war, ended March 31, 1914, for a trade a little over a third of what it was this year, this department spent 827,991,000. Compare the figures: $27,991,000

in 1914 as against $17,408,000 last year. I know my hon. friend is fair enough not to repeat that criticism after he gets the figures, because it is not correct. If I may say so with regard to my predecessor in office, in whose footsteps I have endeavoured to follow, the business of this department has been carried on not only with no great waste but with great economy since this government came into power.

When a member does come to this house with a little advice for the minister which may perhaps take him out of those old trails which he has been following, the minister gets a little annoyed and springs up with a lot of figures on trade and so on. I will guarantee that if he takes the two pages to which I have referred he will be saved a lot of trouble. Knowing the trouble and the anxiety which he has endured during the last few days and the attempts he has made to defend these items and to satisfy the different members who come to him with demands, I have tried to show some places where he can save money in order to allow himself something more to spend in other directions. Apparently my endeavours have been wasted; the minister seemed to get angry, and said we had been spreading false rumours. I have not spread false rumours; I have spent a lot of time over this book and I have pointed out two or three ways in which some little expenditures have been stuffed. I am not going to suggest that the minister ask the Auditor General to look into these matters; perhaps when the Auditor General reads this discussion he will include five or six pages covering the automobiles used by the different departments, just as these telephones are now included. Then we can criticize that expenditure.
I hope the minister will get out of these old paths which he has been following; I hope he will go to his department and say, "I cannot understand why private secretaries have their telephones paid for, or why three or four deputies should require their telephones paid for." I will admit that there is need for some of these telephones, but I think it could be cut down a great deal, and I hope when we discuss these estimates next year we will find a reduction. I am sure a company doing business in the commercial world would look at the overhead charge first of all, and that is what we are endeavouring to do; we believe that we could do a great deal more trade with a smaller overhead than we are carrying. I think I made it plain to the minister, and I hope he understands, that by saving in some directions perhaps he could satisfy some of these other

Supply-Public Works
demands which are made upon him. If the minister will break away from the policy of tu quoque, "Thou also", and never mind what other ministers have done-they have made a great many mistakes and it is only from mistakes made in the past that we can learn to do things better in the future-he will be much 'better off, and that is my only reason for bringing up this matter.
iMr. ELLIOTT: With regard to this matter of supplying telephones to secretaries I understand from the deputy, who has been here much longer than I, that the practice was in vogue when he first entered the department and has been maintained ever since. My hon. friend will agree with me that with the salaries that are being paid and with the cost of living as it is at present, perhaps no official in the public service has such a difficult task as the secretary to a minister. Demands are made upon these secretaries at all hours of the day and night; urgent business of the department necessitates that they be on call all the time, and I hardly think my hon. friend from Kingston, whom I know very well would not want to work an injustice on any official, would suggest that the old practice of supplying these telephones should be done away with. I do not believe that would be in the interests of the public service.

Any business concern
would do it for similar officials.
That is not so.
No.

Suposing we should say to the secretary, "We have decided not to pay for your telephone any longer." I believe that was done by one of my predecessors some years ago, and it lasted just a week. He was not a minister of this government but was a member of the previous administration; he had the idea that this could be dispensed with, and maintained that position for just a week. The secretaries' said, "Very well, if you do not want us to have telephones it is quite all right; we will have them taken out." My hon. friend can readily understand the situation which resulted. I do not want my hon. friend to misunderstand me, 'because1 I think perhaps no member of the house presents his criticisms with a greater desire to be helpful to the government, and I appreciate that fact. I want to get it into his head, if I can, that we have stepped out of the old trails, and because of that fact we have been able to effect the immense economies both in this and other government departments which have occurred since this government took office.

I just rise to correct a remark interjected by the Minister of Railways, who said that ordinary business concerns did the same thing, or words to that effect. I absolutely deny that such is the case. The employees of industrial corporations pay for their own telephones just as they pay for their own breakfasts.

I am sure my hon. friend will allow me to state that just as he personally knows of business concerns which adopt that principle with respect to this class of officials, so do I personally know of corporations which, with respect to the class of officials whose telephones are used far more for the business of the concern than for the business of the individual, pay for these telephones as a matter of business.
That might be done by the national railways, but not in general business practice.

I am not speaking of the national railways but of business concerns with which I am personally familiar. I can speak of them just as my hon. friend can only speak of those with which he is familiar. On the question of principle, I would say that the secretary of any minister must 'be and is in receipt of telephone calls all the time affecting the business of the department and of the minister's office, and in the service of the members. I do not mind confessing that my own practice is to direct that all telegrams coming addressed to me out of office hours shall be telephoned to my secretary. I do not suppose that my hon. friend would desire a minister to 'be answering the phone for hundreds of telegrams which may come in, particularly when there is an agitation in some part of the country during which the people are encouraged to send telegrams' en masse to a minister to influence his course in one direction or another. Really I think it is a pretty small thing to pay for a business telephone which is available for an official out of business hours. That is really what it amounts to; as the Minister of Public Works has said, the experiment of cutting out the practice was once tried and did not succeed very well.

The minister limits the
telephone matter to secretaries. No one, as far as I have heard, has objected to that. The objection is made-I am not making it, but I am only illustrating the objection- to having a whole raft of telephones.

I understood the reference was to secretaries.
Supply-Public Works

Some of them must be justified, but why should three commissioners have telephones? Possibly the secretary should have a telephone, but not the three commissioners. Every little sub-deputy of a department has a telephone while one or two only may be absolutely necessary. My point was that this list should be gone over to find what is necessary to be granted, and what is not necessary. I believe there is one-third of it not necessary. I have brought the matter up to show how economy can be practised and it is apparent that economy could be practised by cutting out some of these telephones. You will find that every member of a commission that comes here has a private telephone. There are several departments in connection with which a great amount of telephoning would not be necessary although that of the minister may be an exception.
Would the minister give me the 'information I asked for at the outset; what proportion of this $100,000 would be allocated to the Rideau Hall telephones?

My hon. friend from Charlotte (Mr. Grimmer) asked for certain information as to why tenders were not invited for post office fittings, including boxes, at St. Stephen. The estimated cost was put at $1,300, in August, 1927. Two tenders were received, one from Joseph MacVay * of St. Stephen, for $1,500, and the other was from George Stewart Ryder, St. Stephen, and was for $1,800. As the appropriation covering this work had been exhausted at that time, the tenders were not accepted, and the security furnished by the tenderers was returned. The item has been noted for consideration.

Supply-Public Works
I would like to ask the minister if it is the intention of the government to proceed at once with the repairs?
There is no vote yet. The item has been noted, along with many others, for the supplementary estimates; that is a matter of consideration in connection with the supplementary estimates.
Is it the intention of the government to wait until such time as they receive tenders that will come within the estimate?

Our difficulty at the
present time is not with the tenders; it is a question of there being no appropriation now. The first thing for the government to consider is whether or not an appropriation for this work will be inserted in the supplementary estimates.
When does the government intend to take this into consideration? Will that come in in the supplementary estimates?
It will be considered.

I think there are other things to be considered at the present time in connection with the matter. This question came up four or five years ago. I was not the one responsible for it, and was not the one that advocated it. No doubt this is a matter for the postal department. They found out that it was absolutely necessary in the interests of the department, to carry on the work, that the premises should be improved. At the same time, there were boxes which the public were willing to pay for. The government, through their engineers, had estimates prepared, and they took into consideration, for the benefit of the department and also for the benefit of the people in that vicinity, the proposition of at once proceeding with the work. That was in 1922 or 1923. It requires only a matter of probably $2,000 or less to cover these alterations. I cannot understand, nor can the people understand, why the Postmaster General does not see his way clear to spend this small matter of $2,000 in the interest of the department, and for the benefit and convenience of the public.
This building was built some thirty-five or forty years ago. No doubt it was then one of the best buildings in that community; it was adequate at that time. The first floor is occupied by the postal department; the second floor is occupied by the customs, and there is a storey and a half above that-Architecture at that time was up in the air,
rather than just floor space. The upper storeys were used by the caretaker. I do not know whether they are using them at the present time or not. The arrangement of the building is such that there is not sufficient space to carry on the postal service satisfactorily. The government themselves decided that in the interests of the department they would make these alterations and the people were led to believe that this work would be done at once. As I said before, something else must be entering into the matter. I hope it is not unjust to the government to suggest that there is something in connection with the tenders; but I have been informed, although I do not know this to be a fact, that the tenders which have been received for making the alterations have been made by Conservatives in the town of St. Stephen. On the other hand I understand there is no one there who happens to be a supporter of the present administration who is equipped for making those alterations. If it is the intention of the government to wait until such time as they can get a tender from one of their own party, they will have to wait until the next generation grows up.
This matter has been hanging fire for the last five years and it is only proper that the government should understand the situation from the point of view of the people in the town. The whole patronage systtm in that county seems to be narrowed down to one person, and if a whole community is going to be subject to one person in respect to alterations and other matters of this kind, it is time that some of the conditions be changed. Here we have one man deciding not only in this matter but in everything else that comes up in connection with any expenditures in Charlotte county. He decides for the county whether or not the government should make these expenditures and it is time that the government take the people in the county into consideration and not one person alone. I hope what I understand to be the case is not so, but indications point that way.
The same thing has come under my observation in connection with two or three requests I have made of the government with respect to certain matters. Some members of the government promised me they would do certain things for the county in respect to little matters. When I would bring a matter before them, they would say: "Yes, I think that is absolutely necessary and I will look after it." But before they look after it, they
Supply-Public Works

have to refer it to the gentleman I have in mind'and what is his answer? He says: "No, if anything is wanted for the county, let them come to me and I will look after it for them." Therefore that is cancelled. I am afraid the same condition exists in regard to making a slight alteration that is so necessary in a public building in order that the work may be carried on in a satisfactory manner in the interest of the postal services. This is not a new budding; it is a building which the government own; it is a building that needs repair. The amount required is only a small one, and therefore I ask: Why carry it over from year to year, going through the farce of asking for tenders and then throwing the whole thing down until the next session? What did the government say in 1921, 1925 and 1926? "The post office is going to be enlarged; there is no difficulty about that; the undertaking is to begin at once." But the day after the ballots were counted, they forgot all about the matter. I do not believe it has any bearing on the town of St. Stephen as far as the voting is cencemed, nevertheless on every platform one of the government's supporters appears before the public making not only that promise 'but others, promises which have never been carried out since this government came into power, and which I do not believe they intend to carry out. Therefore I say in connection with something the government started themselves, in connection with alterations that are necessary for the convenience of the public, for the satisfactory carrying on of the public business, it is up to the government now to spend that paltry sum of $2,000 and not to put the matter off until next year by calling for tenders and then making a farce of it.

So far as I am aware
the reason why a contract was not given out was because the lowest tender was quite a considerable amount above that estimated by our architect as a fair value for the work. I do not mean by that that the architect is always correct as to what these things should cost. Sometimes when we call for tenders and they are near the amount estimated, we have to pay more; but in this case the lowest tender was considerably above the estimate and there was quite a difference between the tenders, one being S300 higher than the other. This is, however, not a large item and while I cannot make any promises to my hon. friend about what will happen to the supple-

mentary estimates, the chance of an item of this kind getting in is much better than that of an item of a larger amount. I think those are all the items that were held up.

Will the minister give me

Under the
general vote for Nova Scotia harbours and rivers, I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Public Works, for the third successive year, the deplorable and inadequate condition of two harbours in the province of Nova Scotia with regard to public service and shipping facilities. As I said, this is the third session I have brought the matter to the attention of the Minister of Public Works, twice to the attention of the present minister, and once to his predecessor.
The first harbour I wish to speak about is that of Port Greville, on the bay of Fundy. The importance of (that 'hanbiour may be realized from the business that passed through the harbour in 1926. Before giving that, let me say that this locality is not served by any other means of transportation. It has no railway facilities, and the business of that locality is absolutely dependent on the shipping facilities provided. To give the committee an idea of the importance of the harbour let me say that in 1926 there passed through the harbour:
5.000.	000 feet of lumber.
31 three and four master schooners repairs.
14 large vessels cleared with lumber.
8 cargoes of piling.
16 cargoes of lumber in smaller vessels.
1.000.	000 feet of lumber shipped in scows.
It amounted, in all, to over 30,000 tons, deadweight, of shipping.
In 1924 or 1925, I am not sure which year, certain repairs were made to the breakwater and certain beach protection work was done. A great deal of money was expended, and it is claimed not properly expended; that is, the expenditure did not give the service it should have provided; a lot of unnecessary work was done, and a lot of necessary work was left undone. The complaint is that the breakwater at this point does not extend out far enough to protect the harbour channel.
Just what was the date of that work?

In 1924 or
1925, I am not sure which, but I think it was 1924. The chief complaint is that the breakwater does not extend far enough out into the harbour to protect the channel, and the result is that with the flow of the tide back and forth, sediment is deposited in the channel; the harbour is gradually filling up, and it will not be long before there will be no harbour there at ali. The result will be that the people of that locality will be unable to ship their products to the markets of the world. I have a communication here from a member of a shipbuilding company in Port Greville, drawing my attention to the fact that this breakwater must be extended by the government, and also that the beach protection, which extends from the breakwater along the shore, must be repaired. He says in conclusion. "Unless something is done soon this harbour will be a thing of the past." It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, in view of all the money that has been lavishly expended by this government in different parts of the Dominion of Canada, and especially in the city of Ottawa, there should surely be enough money in the treasury to protect important public works that require immediate attention in order to enable the people to conduct their shipping business. Not only on that ground, but from the standpoint of good sound business this breakwater should be extended and the beach protection work repaired, because if much mors time is allowed to elapse the cost of these repairs will be double or treble what it would cost to-day. I implore the minister to look into this matter very carefully, and to bring down an item in the supplementary estimates to provide for this service. I admit that this matter has been taken up by some of the persons in that locality with the engineers who are in charge of the government works in the province of Nova Scotia, but apparently the government's engineers there do not appear to understand the significance of what is required at this port. I would urge the government-and I make this plea on behalf of the people of that district-to have this very necessary work done in order that these people may be provided with proper shipping facilities.
The other harbour I wish to bring to the attention of the minister is that of West Advocate. Before speaking of that, I would ask the minister whether an appropriation is to be placed in the supplementary estimates to provide for extending the breakwater at West Advocate. In that case, I shall have nothing further to say, and it will save time.

The name of West
Advocate is familiar to me. The work my

I understand from parties living in that district that the rumour has been circulated there that an estimate amounting to $8,000 would be placed in the supplementary estimates to provide for the extending of the breakwatei at West Advocate. As the minister says that this has not been definitely decided upon, I wish to bring to his attention the situation at this point. West Advocate is also a port on the bay of Fundy, and it has no other transportation facilities beyond the harbour: there is no railroad within a good many miles of this point, and all the lumber, all the pulp, and all the fish of that locality have to be shipped from these two important ports that I have mentioned. At West Advocate, on account of the shortness of the breakwater, vessels cannot get into the harbour, and all the lumber has to be shipped to them in scows and taken out and loaded in the vessels in the stream. The breakwater needs an extension of about 100 feet, I am told, and I would urge the minister to give this matter his serious consideration, because it is impossible for the people living in this district to conduct their shipping business properly and to get their products to market unless the shipping facilities are adequate. I plead with the minister to place in the supplementary estimates a sum sufficient to put these two breakwaters in proper repair, and to extend them at least one hundred feet so the harbours will be protected.

The wharf at Bridgewater is in a deplorable condition, and a car went through the deck last year. I am very grateful indeed that the minister has seen fit to have this work included in the estimates. But I wish to call his attention to another railway wharf at Lunenburg. Both wharves are of equal importance to the communities they serve. The wharf at Lunenburg was constructed at considerable expense, and is the only wharf suitable for ships of any size. The outer portion is absolutely useless; there is no top on it whatsoever, and the bare piles are sticking out in the water. The inner portion is inadequate for the purpose for which it is needed. In the spring large quantities of bait are brought into Lunenburg by the railway, and it has been the custom for the freight cars to be taken on to the wharf and the bait loaded into schooners. Since the wharf is in such bad repair it is necessaiy to cart the bait from the railway yard down to the respective wharves of the fish merchants. At the time I brought the railway wharf at Bridgewater to the minister's attention I also mentioned this wharf. I sincerely hope that he will make provision in the supplementary estimates to look after these much needed repairs. It is not a question of politics. It is a question of saving an investment that is rapidly going to waste.

I wish to call the attention
of the minister to a very small amount that is placed in the estimates for the constituency which I have the honour to represent, and which probably has as long a coast line as any constituency in Nova Scotia. In looking over the different items I find we have an appropriation of only $17,000 to take care of all the breakwaters in Digby-Annapolis. I think the records of the department will show that in the constituency there are as many breakwaters as in any other riding in the province. The neighbouring constituency of Shelbourne-Yarmouth, which is represented by the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has an appropriation of $74,500. I have not any complaint to make, because I have not the slightest doubt that the amount is justified and required; but the same thing applies to my constituency. I look again to the constituency of Antigonish-Guysborough, represented by my hon. friend Mr. William Duff, who sits on the other side of the house, and I find that for his riding the appropriation is $57,600. Why is my constituency discriminated against and allowed only $17,000, while the other two are so generously provided for? I certainly feel that there has been the greatest discrimination, and I am entitled to the same treatment for my constituency as these gentlemen get for theirs. The public service demands it. The government say that they want to do everything they can for the fishing industry in the maritimes, and they have gone to considerable expense appointing a commission to investigate the fisheries problems there. That commission will cost the country a great deal of money. It has made some splendid recommendations which I believe this government will carry out as far as they can. I do not think they can carry them all out, but the commission has recommended that every consideration be given the fishing industry of the maritimes. But that industry cannot be carried on successfully in Nova Scotia without these breakwaters to afford proper protection. In my constituency, more perhaps than in others mentioned, we have the greatest need; the industry there is quite important; yet I am put off with only a trifling sum of $17,000 to take care of breakwaters in that constituency, while others have been liberally looked after. It is in the public interest that the constituency of Digby-Annapolis should be treated just as liberally by this government as such places as Yarmouth and Shelburne or Antigonish-Guysborough. I trust the minister will put a sufficient amount in his estimates to provide for the much needed repairs and improvements in my constituency. There is hardly a breakwater in the constituency which is long enough to enable the fishermen to carry on their vocation satisfactorily; in fact nearly all of them need lengthening, and a great many of them dredging. Some time ago I called the attention of the minister to a petition, which I presented, signed by the residents of Salmon river, Digby county, asking for the dredging of the channel. But no action has been taken; nothing is contained in the estimates for this work. I hope the minister will see that an amount is included in the supplementaries for this dredging in Salmon river. There is also a very important breakwater in my constituency at East Ferry in Digby county, connecting the mainland with Long island and Brier island. It is absolutely necessary that some dredging be done there. The minister has a petition from the municipal council of Digby county asking that a new breakwater be built at this point. It is a very important place; it serves the whole of Long island as well as Brier island.

There is no means of communication except a ferry and the breakwater is in a very bad state of repair. If we do not build a new one there, important repairs will have to be made. Dredging is also necessary and ought to be done this year. I trust the minister will give instructions to the district engineer with regard to the breakwater on the Salmon river and also with regard to one at Victoria beach. Last year I called his attention to the fact that a dredge was working in Digby harbour and I asked him to endeavour if possible to have some work done at Victoria beach, which is an important station at the mouth of Digby harbour. For some reason or other, however, arrangements could not be made. I sincerely trust the minister will give the matter his serious consideration. Do not let him show such partiality when giving out his appropriations for the year. Let him treat us all alike and he will not have very much trouble getting his estimates through. Surely he will take these matters into consideration and try to treat us as liberally as he can.

Much as I should like to get my estimates through easily, I cannot get more money than the treasury board will allow me or council will pass. I know my hon. friend will revise his statements as regards discrimination when he considers what has been done for one of his colleagues. If he will look at Queens-Lunenburg he will see how much has been spent there.
A good many of the items for Queens-Lunenburg relate to works which have been begun already. They are revotes.
They were represented by the same man last year.

I thank the minister for
treating my constituency as generously as he has done, although I do not mean to say that he has given us everything that we need.
At least you will say I have given the things that are urgent.

The minister has treated the constituency fairly; I will say that. But there is one matter to which I wish to call his attention-something that has arisen since these estimates were compiled. I refer to the harbour of Liverpool. Liverpool is a town of 3,000 and is the capital of Queens county. Since the house convened, thanks to the activities of the government of Nova Scotia, Liverpool has been assured of a newsprint mill of 200 tons capacity daily. This mill is being set up there largely because the power facilities at that point are the best in the

province, and the mill will be situate at tidewater. The harbour is open the year round. But if the venture is to be a complete success it will be necessary for the department to cooperate with the provincial government and with the company in improving the harbour facilities. There is a sand bar across the harbour. It was dredged some years ago but it has again accumulated to such an extent that large vessels cannot use the port. I will ask the minister to give every consideration to the needs of this port, not merely because it is the port of the capital of Queens county but because it is destined to be one of the ports of Nova Scotia. May I ask him to make the fullest survey of the harbour with a view to having everything done which is necessary to make this port what it is destined to be.

Those of us from the west are not in a position to vote intelligently on these items; we must take the word of hon. gentlemen from the maritimes. I repeat now what I have said before with respect to these grants for harbours: it seems to me that the proper thing to do would be to increase the indemnity to the provincial government. Go back over a period of years and see what it has cost to keep up these harbours. In my opinion the provinces could expend this money to better advantage than we can. The members of the provincial legislatures are more closely in touch with the situation and they would know what they were dealing with. If you take the records of the three maritime provinces you will see that they have had efficient and economical administration; I know enough about the maritimes to be able to say that. I think

suggest that we change the British North America Act and give control of navigation to the provinces?

I do not know that
that would be involved at all, although I am not a lawyer. However, I would not allow a little thing like the British North America Act to stand in the way.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But if there is one
matter which is truly national in its character surley it is navigation.

I do not know that
that has anything to do with my proposition, and I do not know that it would involve any change in the British North America Act, although I cannot say that with authority. If the administration of these matters were turned over to the maritime provinces my contention is that they could expend the money to much better advantage, more efficiently and more economically. The members of the legislative assemblies of those provinces are in a much better position to deal with these questions.

But the members of
this house from the maritime provinces should be able to deal with them.

Yes, but the members
from all the other parts of the country have a responsibility, and in this case I suggest that the responsibility should rest entirely upon the members of the legislative assembly.
I think the hon. member for Mackenzie is so accustomed to the efficient government of the province of Saskatchewan that he expects to find the same condition in other parts of the Dominion.

With regard to the
legal problem I suggest that we have a new doctor of laws in the house, and we might put it up to him.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES AND ATLANTIC CANAL AND POWER COMPANY, LIMITED
speechtext:
I move, seconded by Mr. Tummon:
That Bill No. 152, respecting the Great Lakes and Atlantic Canal and Power Company, Limited, be not now read a second time but that it be read a second time this day six months' hence.

Great Lakes and Power Company
I wish to raise the question whether the second reading of this bill is in order inasmuch as it is within the four corners of a reference to the supreme court on the St. Lawrence waterways question by the following order in council which the Prime Minister laid on the table on the 31st January, and the issues covered by this bill are sub judice and relate to the jurisdiction of the federal and provincial authorities over navigation- the surplus waters, who owns the bed of these streams and the banks and rapids, and generally the power question as follows:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated 17th January, 1928, from the Minister of Justice, submitting that at the Dominion-provincial conference, held at Ottawa in the month of November, 1927, the premiers of certain of the provinces questioned the right of the Dominion to dispose of water-powers brought into being by the erection of Dominion works for the improvement of navigation, and asserted a right on the part of the province to dispose of any such water-powers within the limits of the provinces.
This bill is largely a power proposition and it also proposes to give over to a private company a canal running from Cornwall through Montreal. If the bill goes through there will be no St. Lawrence waterways. It will mean that t'he Canadian section will be out of the question for all time. The bill deals with the very questions which are now before the supreme court. All the questions involved in the preamble of it and indeed in the whole bill are now sub judice and I should like hon. members from Ontario to understand that if this particular proposition goes through, we shall have no St. Lawrence waterway. This is the question involved in the reference to the supreme court:
The committee, therefore, on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice, advise that, pursuant to the powers in that behalf conferred by section 60 of the Supreme Court Act, Your Excellency may be pleased to refer to the Supreme Court of Canada for hearing and consideration the following questions.
If hon. members will look at the questions involved in this particular bill they will see that it involves the very question of the jurisdiction of the province as regards not only water powers but the construction of a canal. Therefore it covers questions that are now before the supreme court. It has been announced by one of the provinces that it is going to carry the matter to the privy council, the court of last appeal. There was a debate in the house on the 10th April in connection with the iSt. Lawrence waterway and the Prime Minister suggested that the bill should stand until the papers were brought down. If hon. members will look at the correspondence between Mr. Kellogg, Secretary of the United States, and the Ambassador at Washington of the government of Canada, and the government of Canada, they will see that it covers the very questions that are involved in this bill, namely, the right of the federal authorities on the one hand and the right of the state or province on the other, the international question, the federal division of authority with the provinces', and other questions regarding the canalization of the new St. Lawrence waterway. Further they are starting to divert water at Chicago right down to the Mississippi river for a canal there. Then there is a canal proposition at Ogdens-burg going down to Albany. The third is the proposition before the house to-night for a canal running from Cornwall through the deep sections of the Canadian waterway to Beauharnois and right down to Montreal, and they propose to construct a private canal and upset all the settled canal policy of Canada for the past fifty years. I do not know what is to become of the port of Montreal if this bill goes through and if everybody is to have the right to divert water right from lake Michigan all the way down the great lakes to Montreal for canal and power purposes. Among the questions referred to the supreme court was this:
]. Has the province any proprietary interest in flowing waters within the province-
In this case the water is wholly within the province of Quebec:
-and if so, what is the nature of such interest?
That is covered by the preamble of the bill and the sections that follow. The next question submitted to the supreme court was:
2.	Does the ownership by the province of the bed of any stream whether such bed be level or sloping, give to the province the ownership of water-powers?
It has always been upheld that subject to the rights of navigation, the surplus waters, the bed of the river, the banks and rapids belong to the provinces. The question raised by this bill is already sub judice before the supreme court and no doubt it will be appealed to the privy council. This same question came up in this house two years ago in connection with the Morrisburg dam. The province of Ontario wanted to build a dam at Morrisburg and develop power wholly within Ontario, and the Minister of the Interior read an opinion in the house in the year 1926 to the effect that there was no doubt that so far as navigation was concerned the interest of the Dominion in international streams was paramount, but that the surplus waters and the bed of the river and the banks

Great Lakes and Power Company
arid rapids belong to the province after the rights of navigation were satisfied. The province applied under the Boundary Waterways Protection Act for power to build that dam, and plans were filed by Sir Adam Beck on behalf of the Ontario Hydro Commission and the Ontario government, but the application stood for three or four years, and never was granted. If that dam had been built, it would have been of benefit to the whole of eastern Ontario. It is true that the power to be developed under this bill which is now before us is from a river that is wholly on the Canadian side in Quebec, but what about the rights of the people farther up the lakes? What about the several other canals? And if the province of Quebec is to have this right, Ontario will also claim the same right, and so will the state of Illinois, New York, and other states, and you will find yourself on very dangerous ground. To continue with the questions referred to the supreme court:
2.	Does the ownership by the province of the bed of any stream, whether such bed be level or sloping, give to the province the ownership of water-powers:
(a)	created thereupon by dominion works for the improvement of navigation; or
(b)	existing thereupon by nature?
3.	Has the province any proprietary interest in or legislative control over:
(a) the canals, with lands and water-power connected therewith, and the lake and river improvements which were conveyed to the dominion by section 108, schedule 3, of the British North America Act, 1867, or in or over the disposal of any water-powers created thereby or existing thereupon from time .to time; or
_ (b) water-powers created by works for the improvement of navigation constructed by or under the authority of the dominion since confederation; or
(e) works constructed wholly for power purposes by the dominion out of moneys appropriated by parliament for such purpose?
Part of this canal is for navigation purposes :
If so, what is the nature of such interest or control ?
4.	Has the dominion exclusive legislative power to regulate waters for the purposes of navigation:
(a)	in navigable waters; and
(b)	in non-navigable waters?
5.	Where the dominion, for navigation purposes, expropriates or uses any part of the bed of any stream vested in the province, is the province entitled to any compensation for such expropriation or use?
6.	Has the dominion the exclusive legislative control over and proprietary interest in water-powers brought into being by works authorized by parliament to be erected in an international stream for the purpose of carrying out an agreement between Canada and any foreign country looking to the creation of joint works for the improvement of navigation in such streams?
If not, what are the powers and rights of the province with regard to such water-powers? [Mr. Church.1
That is the very question whicn this bill brings up. To continue:
7.	Where the bed of a navigable stream is owned by the province or by a private individual, is the title of such owner subordinate to the public right of navigation, and to the provisions of any statute which may be enacted from time to time by parliament, within the powers conferred by section 91 (10) of the British North America Act, 1867?
In conclusion, I wish to quote May's Parliamentary Procedure, at page 709, in regard to what principle is involved in the second reading of a bill. He says:
The second reading of a private bill corresponds with the same stage in other bills, and in agreeing to it the house affirms the general principle, or expediency, of the measure. There is, however, a distinction between the second reading of a public and of a private bill, which should not be overlooked. A public bill being founded on reasons of state policy, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, accepts and affirms those reasons: but the expediency of a private bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the house, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill, conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee. Where, irrespective of such facts, the principle is objectionable-
As it is in this case, because the question is sub judice:
7 the house will not consent to the second reading; but otherwise, the expediency of the measure is usually left for the consideration of the committee.
The time to enter a protest against the principle of a bill is on the second reading, and I am opposed to this bill in principle. I say further that in view of the order in council which I have read, this bill should not be gone on with on grounds of law and of public policy, and in view also of the exchange of correspondence between Washington and Ottawa on the whole question of the St. Lawrence deep waterway. The interests of navigation are paramount.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES AND ATLANTIC CANAL AND POWER COMPANY, LIMITED
speechtext:
On the point of order, if the question before the courts was exactly the same as the one that is being debated by the house, I would have no hesitation in saying, as I have said in similar circumstances, that the question, being sub judice, was not debatable before the house. But it is not the same question.
As regards the general point raised by the hon. gentleman, I find, according to Bourinot:
The Speaker will not give a decision upon a constitutional question, nor decide a question of law, though the same may be raised on a point of order or privilege.
That disposes, I think, of the question of the point of order.

Great Lakes and Power Company
The question now before the house is that this bill, respecting the Great Lakes and Atlantic Canal and Power Company, Limited, be read a second time, and in amendment thereto Mr. Church moves that the said bill be not now read a second time, but that it be read a second time this day six months hence. The question is on the amendment.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals):	Just before the
question is put, while my views on the bill would probably coincide with those of the hon. member who has moved the six months hoist, it is customary to allow petitioners for private bills to appear before a committee of the house and there state their views, what they want, and why they want it, and the normal course to follow in the case of a bill of this character would be to refer it to the select standing committee on railways and canals. While I cannot predict the outcome, the very fact that the six months' hoist has been moved indicates that the bill would be very carefully scrutinized by that committee, and I submit that that work can be done very much better by a committee of the house than by our summarily disposing of the matter on the second reading of the bill. I think we would all agree that we reserve our right to destroy the bill on the third reading even if it does come back from the committee. The work of the house in connection with a bill of this kind can be done much more conveniently by one of the standing committees, and for that reason I am opposed to the six months' hoist.
Mr. G. R. GEARY' (South Toronto):	I
think one would not take exception as a general rule to what the minister has just said. The ordinary course is to allow such a bill to be passed on to a committee in order that it may be explained there by its promoters, but that, of course, is subject to consideration of the general situation which follows the passing of the second reading, that thereby the principle of the bill is more or less adopted. It seems to me that this bill can have no possible chance of success. On principle it is wrong in the circumstances, because we have the very recent declaration of the government that the whole question of the St. Lawrence waterway is to be considered; that not only have negotiations been entered into and correspondence passed between Washington and Ottawa, but that the government has the matter under consideration. I have forgotten the exact language used, but that is the effect of it. This bill is diametrically opposed to any fair consideration of the St. Lawrence waterway proposition. If this bill were passed granting the promoters power to construct the projected canal, it would be an absolute bar to the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway as a national undertaking. One has only to look at the powers contained in section 17 and the other powers scattered throughout the bill to realize that it is not at all the sort of measure which the house should consider at the moment. It is directly opposed to ownership by the Dominion of the deepened waterway when and if it be completed. The bill is studded with provisions that will interfere with and endanger action by this house on the St. Lawrence waterway project.
Now, we have not reached the position where the St. Lawrence waterway deepening can be discussed, but I think I may express it as the general feeling of the house that this great undertaking will come eventually. So the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has put it, and so most of us in the house believe. But to place in the hands of private owners navigation rights through the St. Lawrence is beyond belief. I do not know of a case where such rights have been granted, either by the federal or the provincial authorities, to private individuals. Nor should they be so granted, because as a highway on land should be free to the passerby, so should the road by water be free to those who seek to use it. No private corporation is entitled to come to this house and ask to be given powers which will override the natural rights of the people to the ownership of their own water courses.

maintopic: GREAT LAKES AND ATLANTIC CANAL AND POWER COMPANY, LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I associate myself with
the mover of this amendment (Mr. Church). We have spent a large amount of money in getting reports on the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway. The government has not declared its policy with respect to the project, but it has submitted certain questions of federal and provincial jurisdiction to the supreme court. The province of Quebec is not the only province interested in the result; Ontario and the western provinces are also concerned. The province of Quebec may have the right to grant incorporation to this company which proposes to build a canal, but the canal would really form part and parcel of the St. Lawrence waterway. The deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway is not only an interprovincial matter, it is international.
There is sufficient in the preamble of the bill to show just exactly what-is intended by the promoters. The principle involved is absolutely contrary to what this parliament should sanction. The United States have treaty rights with regard to the navigation of the St. Lawrence, and this canal, if constructed, would very materially interfere with those rights. This would bring up the question of damages and other collateral matters. I am strongly opposed to the bill on principle, for it affects the question of navigation; and, further, the question of federal and provincial jurisdiction, which at present is under consideration by the supreme court. This is simply trying to get certain powers which will create a complication when we come to deal with the whole question. The preamble itself is quite wide. It says:
Whereas a petition has been presented by the Great Lakes and Atlantic Canal and Power Company, Limited, a body politic and corporate,

Great Lakes and Power Company
duly incorporated under the Companies Act, chapter seventy-nine of the revised statutes of Canada, 1906, hereinafter called "the company", praying that it may be authorized to construct and operate a deep waterway from the western end of lake St. Francis at or near the town of Cornwall in the county of Stormont, in the province of Ontario to Hungry bay in the county of Beauharnois in the province of Quebec, and to build a canal from said Hungry bay to a point at or near Melocheville, in the said county at Lake St. Louis, and a deep waterway through lake St. Louis to a point at or near Caughnawaga in the county of La Prairie; or by an alternative route to build a canal from Lake St. Francis at Hungry bay in the county of Beauharnois, through the said county of Beauharnois and thence through the counties of Chateauguay and La Prairie, to some point on La Prairie basin, in the latter county; to create a deep waterway from La Prairie basin to deep water in the harbour of Montreal, so as to make and complete throughout the entire distance from Cornwall aforesaid to the harbour of Montreal as aforesaid, a navigable canal-
And so on.
That is involved in the St. Lawrence scheme, and, as I say, it is merely an attempt to anticipate action in regard to the entire question. If this bill were passed it would thwart the whole scheme. I am opposed to it on principle and I shall vote for this amendment. No doubt if it went to the committee there would be ample opportunity to discuss it, but I do not think it deserves the consideration that was shown a similar bill last year. On principle that bill was wrong but it was sent to a committee and it was there for a considerable time before it was killed. I am satisfied to support this amendment and I think it would be the part of wisdom for the house to accept it.

speechtext: In-as much as I am paired with the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) and therefore am unable to vote, our pair being binding at all times, I rise now to say that I am strongly opposed to this bill-as strongly opposed as anyone can be. are part and parcel of the railway, operated and used 'by the railway, and the Public Works department has nothing whatever to do with them.

One of the reasons why we are not taking all the wharves over, as I answered my hon. friend, is that there is a difference between those which are public wharves and those which are mostly railway wharves. That information is
quite correct so far as it goes, but it is not strictly accurate in this respect; the railway wharves are used exclusively in connection with the railway. It is quite true that the coastal boats land their freight and their passengers.

say that the vessels going to the Magdalen islands are railway vessels?

will wait a moment I will make myself clear. It is quite true that the coastal boats use these wharves, but they use them to land passengers and freight which come over the railway. Any local freight
(Mr. W. A. Black. [
coming by these boats is infinitesimal, probably not more than one per cent. These wharves are strictly railway wharves. Are
those the only reasons that the minister's department now gives for the building of a new wharf in that locality?
It is reported to us to be cheaper and better. Those are the reasons.

I have
taken the matter up with the Minister of Public Works and he has made t'he statement that the petition states so-and-so. I know of no petition that has been passed through my district except one and that is a petition in opposition to the new * site of the wharf, a petition which the minister has in his possession and which is signed by 153 residents of the district and vicinity which the proposed wharf would serve. The question came up in 1921 and the same engineer who has handed in the report which the minister today reads, reported that the site of the existing wharf was the site that should be chosen. The people in that vicinity claim that this new wharf is an unnecessary expenditure of public money. We need public money. I make the statement that I am not opposed to the expenditure of public money in my constituency and I say that we have not so far received a sufficient quota of public moneys that are expended in Nova Scotia and in the Dominion generally. The county of Richmond is entitled to far more money but that money should be expended properly. It should not be expended as this $4,200 is to be expended in Richmond where it is being spent wholly and solely for political purposes. It is being spent in order that a vacant farm in that constituency may be sold at a better price. That is the whole statement. There are not six people in that community who want this new public wharf. As my hon. friend knows, his department must function when they are asked to do so by departmental heads, and that is the reason why such a report is in the department to-day. I have here a petition which was presented to the hon. Minister of Public Works, signed by 153 residents of that district. They are not all of one political faith, but of all political faiths. There are only three or four people in that district who have not signed this petition. Those people have signed because they want public money spent for public service. They do not want to see public money wasted. They want the present wharf which was built in 1921 to be repaired by this government. They do not want the new wharf built, and the minister knows that full well. This is the petition which has been signed by 153 persons of that district:
We, the undersigned residents of Soldier's Cove, Grand River and vicinity, humbly petition your department to reconsider the matter of constructing a wharf at Soldier's Cove, opposite the site of the present wharf, for the following reasons:
Whereas, the location on the opposite side of the harbour is not suitable for shipping-[DOT]
They make the statement openly, that it is not suitable for shipping. Further, let me state that the only marine captain in that district, Captain D. L. Stewart, a man who has sailed the Bras d'Or lakes for the last twenty-five or thirty years, is the man who signs second on this list, and he should know whether the above statement in the petition is right. The petition goes on:

-is not suitable for shipping, because of its exposure to the Bras d'Or lakes, for a distance of twenty miles, with north and northwest winds prevailing;
Whereas, ships could not moor at suggested site of new wharf, with above-mentioned winds prevailing;
Whereas, wharf site would have to be purchased and the department put to the expense of building a new wharf, where one now exists;
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, only one or two people in that whole district are interested in the purchase of this site. It goes on:
Whereas, a highway would have to be constructed for a distance of half a mile;
Imagine it! A new highway will have to be built although a highway already exists leading to the present wharf. It goes on:
Whereas, the highway from suggested site would be so steep as to make it impractical to haul more than one-third the average load, from the wharf to the main highway;
